text:
ANNOTATION of the course  
Modern Web Technologies and User Interface Develop-
ment (Современные веб-технологии и разработка 
пользовательского интерфейса) 
Compiled by M.E. Abramyan, Associate Professor of the Department of Algebra and Dis-
crete Mathematics, 
Senior Lecturer of the Department of Mathematical Modeling P.A. Oganisyan. 
1. Program title, degree, study mode 
Direction of training: 02.03.02 Theoretical Computer Science and Information Technologies 
(Фундаментальная информатика и информационные технологии) 
Graduate qualification (degree): Bachelor 
Full-time form of education 
2. Total load 
5 credits (180 hours), of which in the 4th semester 48 hours of lectures, 32 hours of la-
boratory studies and 28 hours of independent work, in the 5th semester 36 hours of lectures, 18 
hours of laboratory studies and 18 hours of independent work. 
 
3. Course sequencing 
Academic discipline “02.03.02 Theoretical Computer Science and Information Technologies 
(Фундаментальная информатика и информационные технологии) " (2 course, 4 semester, 3 
course, 5 semester) refers to a part of a block of disciplines (modules) formed by participants in 
educational relations, and is a compulsory discipline. 
To study this academic discipline (module), knowledge, skills and abilities are required, 
formed by the previous discipline “Basics of Programming (Основы программирования)". 
The list of subsequent academic disciplines for which knowledge, skills and abilities are re-
quired, formed by this academic discipline: “ Computer Graphics (Компьютерная графика) " 
(4th year, 7th semester). The knowledge and skills gained in the course of studying this disci-
pline can be used to solve professional problems in research, scientific production and design 
activities, in particular, when developing programs as part of graduation qualification works. 
4. Course aims and objectives 
Developing students' knowledge, skills and abilities related to the development of a user in-
terface, mastering one of the libraries of visual components intended for developing a graphical 
interface (as an example of such a library, the Windows.Forms library is used, which is part of 
the standard class library of the .NET Framework) , the formation of knowledge and skills in 
working with multi-paradigm languages using the example of the Ruby language, the formation 
of skills and knowledge of software development using the TDD paradigm, the formation of 
skills for developing client -server applications on the Ruby on Rails platform, mastering the de-
velopment methodology through testing, the formation of skills in describing the application 
domain using Active Record models. 
Tasks:  
• studying the principles of developing user interfaces for console and window graphical 
applications; mastering the technology of visual design of graphical interfaces (using the 
example of the Visual Studio 2008-2015 environment); 
• mastering the technology of developing event -driven programs, studying the main types 
of events, including events from the keyboard, events from the mouse, events that pro-
vide the implementation of the Drag & Drop technology; 
• study of various control components implemented in the standard Windows.Forms library 
in the form of classes (in particular, forms, single -line and multi -line input fields, check 
boxes, radio buttons, combo boxes and drop -down lists, grouping components, compo-
nents that provide navigation through the file system, components that provide work with 
menus, toolbars, status bars), as well as various non -visual components used in the im-
plementation of user interfaces (timers, standard dialog boxes); 
• studying the capabilities of the GDI + graphic library used in the development of graphic 
applications, mastering the basic techniques of developing applications for editing text 
and graphic information; 
• learning the basic tools of the Ruby programming language and the Ruby on Rails 
framework; 
• study of tools for the development of test coverage of applied software; 
• study of the Active Record design pattern through an example of its implementation with-
in the Ruby on Rails platform 
• studying methods and tools creating client web applications 
5. Intended learning outcomes 
As a result of mastering the discipline, the student must have the following knowledge, 
skills and abilities: 
To understand and analyze:  
• basic principles of user interface development;  
• principles of functioning of event -driven programs, the main types of events (including 
events from the mouse, from the keyboard, events related to the Drag & Drop technolo-
gy); 
• the roles of forms, controls, and non-visual components in the user interface; 
• basic types of controls and their features;  
• the main components of the graphics library GDI +; 
• features of the Ruby language and the Ruby on Rails framework 
• methodologies for developing automated tests 
• tools for generating a domain model using the Active Record design pattern 
• tools and methods for developing modern web applications 
To create and to be able to: 
• develop event-driven programs;  
• use appropriate controls (single -line and multi -line input fields, checkboxes and radio 
buttons, regular and drop -down lists, grouping components, components that provide 
navigation through the file system, components that provide work with menus, toolbars, 
status bars), their properties and methods for solving typical tasks related to the develop-
ment of the user interface; 
• customize drawing tools: pens and brushes; create Graphics objects and use their methods 
to draw various shapes; use the classes of the GDI + library to solve typical tasks related 
to loading, changing and saving images; 
• work with text as an additional graphic element, set properties of the Font class, format 
text; 
• use various graphic resources in a Windows application: cursors, icons, images;  
• develop software based on the TDD paradigm 
• design and develop client -server applications on the Ruby on Rails platform within the 
MVC concept 
• develop unit and integration tests for Ruby on Rails applications 
• generate a domain model using ORM Active Record 
• design and develop client web applications 
  
To apply:  
• in the application of technologies for visual interface development; 
• in Ruby programming 
• in writing automated tests 
• in the design and development of Web applications 
The process of studying the discipline is aimed at the formation of the following competen-
cies: 
  ОПК-4. Able to participate in the development of technical documentation for software products 
and complexes using standards, norms and rules, as well as in the management of projects for the 
creation of information systems at the stages of the life cycle 
  Indicators 
  ОПК-4.1. Applies standards, norms and rules in the development of technical documentation for 
software products and complexes 
  ОПК-4.2. Manages projects for the creation of information systems 
6. Course content 
Section 1. Development of the user interface 
Topic 1.1. Basic techniques for developing an interface for console and window ap-
plications. Window forms and main types of events 
The structure of the console application and the namespaces connected to it. Formatted 
output, in particular the use of escape sequences. DriveInfo, StringBuilder, and Environment 
classes. Using command line parameters. 
Basic techniques for developing events -driven programs. Bind an event to a handler (in 
design mode and programmatically), detach the handler from the event, and then reattach it. The 
structure of a graphical Windows application and its elements. Features of applications that use 
multiple forms, different ways to customize the appearance of forms and the modes of their dis-
play on the screen. Interaction of forms within one application. Dialog box settings and methods 
for displaying standard dialogs. 
Sharing handlers among multiple components. Using an exception handling mechanism 
to handle input errors. Keyboard acceleration options (default buttons, acceleration keys, and us-
ing the KeyPress event). Handling mouse events. Capturing the mouse by a component and 
problems caused by such a capture. V arious aspects of the Drag & Drop drag mode (starting the 
Drag & Drop mode and various options for its completion, actions when dragging to an invalid 
target, additional selection of the source and target, and setting the cursor appearance in drag 
mode). 
Topic 1.2. The main visual components and features of their use 
Peculiarities of working with input fields (TextBox components). Component activation 
(gain and loss of input focus), component traversal order. Processing erroneous data at the level 
of a separate input field and the form as a whole. A mechanism for generating error messages 
based on the use of the ErrorProvider component. CheckBox and CheckedListBox components 
that implement checkbox and checkbox group controls. Methods for checking and changing the 
state of flags, and the peculiarities of using flags that take three states. ComboBox and ListBox 
components that implement combo box and list box controls. Methods for performing standard 
actions on list items (adding, deleting, inserting, changing the order, etc.). Actions, allowing to 
implement drag and drop of list items in drag & drop mode. Components providing data scroll-
ing (TrackBar, HScrollBar, VScrollBar). 
Classes related to dates and times (the DateTime, TimeSpan classes, and the non -visual 
Timer component). Stopwatch implementation options; actions that display the clock and stop-
watch on the taskbar when the application window is minimized. Specifics of using cursors 
(Cursor and Cursors classes) and icons (Icon class) in an application. Embedding graphic re-
sources into the application. Grouping components Panel and SplitContainer, their features. The 
parent-to-child relationship and the order of the child components in the form or other container 
component (Z-order). 
Classes that provide visualization of the computer's file structure: DriveListBox, 
DirListBox and FileListBox. Using the Windows registry to store information about the state of 
the application and then restore it (the Registry and RegistryKey classes). 
Topic 1.3. Working with graphics. Additional user interface tools 
Classes for working with color (Color, KnownColor, ColorTranslator). Basic actions with 
graphic files (creation, saving and loading). Features of the main graphics classes: Image, Bit-
map, Graphics, PictureBox. Tracking the current coordinates of the image, drawing with a fine 
pen (using the Pen and Pens classes), and cleaning up the image. Drawing with a colored pen of 
arbitrary thickness (Pen and ColorDialog classes) and drawing straight lines with the ability to 
display the current position of the drawn line in an inverse color (the DrawReversibleLine meth-
od of the ControlPaint class). Setting the background color (SolidBrush class) and drawing rec-
tangles and ellipses (using Graphics class methods) in normal mode and in transparency mode. 
Undo the last graphic operation, set the color using the eyedropper tool, 
Creation and customization of the main menu of the application (component MenuStrip). 
Basic actions with text files (creating, saving, loading, displaying a request to save changes made 
to the text). Features of the dialog components SaveFileDialog and OpenFileDialog and the mul-
ti-line variant of the TextBox component. Creation of special menu commands (checkboxes and 
radio buttons) and third -level menu groups. Standard text editing commands and their inclusion 
in the main menu (MenuStrip component) and in the editor's context menu (ContextMenuStrip 
component). Creation and customization of the application toolbar (ToolStrip component) and its 
elements: ordinary shortcut buttons, checkboxes and radio buttons. Adding images to the appli-
cation resource file and linking the added images to buttons and menu commands. Creation and 
configuration of the application status panel (StatusStrip component) and its label elements. Us-
ing the ToolTip component. The RichTextBox component and its font and paragraph formatting 
capabilities. Determining the position of the cursor in the text and saving the text in various for-
mats. 
Features of multi -document interface applications (MDI applications). Interaction of the 
main and child forms (child -forms), ways of implementing standard actions on child forms (op-
tions for placement on the screen, displaying a list of child -forms in the menu, simultaneous 
closing of all child -forms, etc.). Scaling an image in a child form and scrolling through the con-
tents of the form using the keyboard. Features related to the creation of components during pro-
gram execution. Setting identification data for the developed application (application name, its 
short description, information about the author, version number). 
Questions for self-study 
The DataGridView table component and its capabilities related to setting the properties of 
its columns. Displaying a splash window with special properties (no title, translucency, etc.) on 
the screen. Ways of early termination of the program. The Sleep method of the Thread class and 
the DoEvents method of the Application class. ProgressBar component (progress bar). 
Section 2. The Ruby Language and the TDD Paradigm 
Topic 2.1. An introduction to dynamically typed languages and Ruby 
Ruby language and development environment. Ruby interpreter. Code analyzers, Rubo-
cop. Ruby data types. Kinds of strings in Ruby. Character strings, literal freezing. Numeric data 
types. Arrays and associative arrays. Conditional operators. Cycles. Closures: blocks, procs, 
lambda expressions. Functions. Exception Handling. Reading and writing files, encoding control. 
Modules, Classes, Monkey Patching. Ruby inheritance. Rake. Gem concept. Gemfile, Bundler, 
installation and update of modules. Build and publish packages via Rubygems. Assessment of 
the cognitive complexity and quality of the code. Project management, introduction to version 
control systems. 
Topic 2.2 Test-Driven Development 
Concept and basic principles of TDD. Types of tests. Unit, integration, system tests. Pre-
paring test data. Load testing methods. BDD concept. Test automation tools. Automated applica-
tion deployment. CI / CD. 
Section 3. Ruby on Rails and Web Programming 
Topic 3.1. Developing Web Applications on the Ruby on Rails Platform 
Simplest web applications using Sinatra. Layered Rack Architecture. Parsing HTML and 
XML documents, Nokogiri. Ruby on Rails (RoR) framework. Basic principles of RoR. Unit and 
Integration Tests. Scfolding in Rails. Development environment and test environment. The struc-
ture of the web application. Model -View-Controller concept. RoR MVC implementation. Con-
trollers and routing. Filters in controllers. 
Topic 3.2. Description of the subject area using Active Record. 
Model in MVC concept. Active Record as a paradigm and as a gem in RoR. ORM con-
cept. Migration concept, change, up and down functions. Using rake to get things done. Data 
types in Active Record. Configuring access to the DBMS using yml files. The role of environ-
ments in configuration settings. Active Record query interfaces: create, search, edit, delete data. 
Scope concept. Active Record events. Data validation. Data security methods. Encryption in Ac-
tive Record. Types of links between models. Transaction concept. Locking records and tables. 
Multi-threaded data access. Analyzing the efficiency of ORM queries. N + 1 query problem. Pro-
totyping user data access with Active Admin. Automatic generation of migrations. Sorts and fil-
ters in Active Admin. Background processes and scheduled tasks in Rails. Active Job. 
Topic 3.3. Designing and developing client -side web applications on the Ruby on 
Rails platform 
Representation tools. Embedded Ruby, HAML, SLIM templating engines. Separation of 
the client and server parts. Rails Assets Pipeline. Assembling the client side of the application. 
Webpacker. Fundamentals of СSS and SCSS. Headless browsers and their role in automated ap-
plication testing. Integration Test Scripts, Capybara. API concept. HTTP verbs: GET, POST, 
PUT, DELETE, PA TCH. Other HTTP verbs. HTTP codes. Web server concept, HTTP REST re-
quest communication and SOAP services. Designing REST services. JSON format. Ensuring the 
security of data transmission. Formation of the signature of the request. Session concept. Built -in 
RoR tools for shaping sessions. External data validation. Using typed errors. ActionCable, Web-
sockets. RoR logging. Load testing of Web applications. Deploying applications to RoR, 
7. Basic educational technologies 
When conducting lectures and laboratory classes, the following educational technologies are 
used: 
• multimedia lectures; 
• electronic forms of control; 
• self-testing of students. 
The educational process is based on the concept of competence -based learning, focused on 
the formation of a specific list of professional competencies, updating the theoretical knowledge 
obtained. The deployment of a competency -based learning model presupposes the widespread 
use of innovative ways of organizing the educational process, including the use of a project -
based learning method, technologies of guided independent learning, including a point -rating 
system, as well as the introduction of an online support system for students' out-of-class work. 
8. Formative and Interim assessment methods  
Current control: laboratory work, testing. 
Mid-term control: completing additional tasks and writing tests. 
Final certification: credit, set based on the results of work in the semester.

name: Protection of Information in Networks (Защита информации в сети)
text:
ANNOTATION of the course  
Protection of Information in Networks (Защита информации в сети) 
 
 Compiled by: Associate Professor of the Department of Informatics and Computational 
Experiment Nesterenko V .A. 
1. Program title, degree, study mode 
Direction of training: 02.03.02 Theoretical Computer Science and Information Technologies 
(Фундаментальная информатика и информационные технологии) 
Graduate qualification (degree): Bachelor 
Full-time form of education 
2. Total load 
5 credits (180 hours), of which 36 hours of lectures, 36 hours of laboratory studies and 108 
hours of independent work 
3. Course sequencing 
Academic discipline “Protection of Information in Networks (Защита информации в сети)” 
(4th year, 7th semester) refers to a part of a block of disciplines (modules) formed by participants 
in educational relations, and is an optional discipline. 
To study this academic discipline, knowledge, skills and abilities are required, formed by 
the previous disciplines: “Basics of Programming (Основы программирования)" and "Computer 
Networks (Компьютерные сети)". 
The knowledge and skills acquired by students should be sufficient for independent study 
of various methods of creating reliable software and acquiring system programming skills, taking 
into account the peculiarities of the system architecture; methods of protecting programs and iden-
tifying various kinds of "bookmarks" in the preparation of the final qualifying work. 
4. Course aims and objectives 
Formation of knowledge and skills that form the theoretical and practical founda-
tion necessary for the use of existing and development of new means of detecting viola-
tions and protecting information in networks.  
Tasks:  
- problems and directions of development of hardware and software for information protection 
in networks; 
- application criteria for assessing the security of systems; 
- development and use modern methods of detecting network violations;  
5. Intended learning outcomes 
As a result of mastering the discipline, the student must have the following knowledge, skills 
and abilities: 
To understand and analyze:  
• aboutbasic concepts of information security; 
• basic principles of organization and functioning of systems for detecting security violations 
in networks; 
• the main ways to detect attempts to breach security in networks. 
• the most common types of network attacks and network security violations. 
• capabilities of modern systems for detecting security violations in networks. 
• Problems and directions of development in the field of modern methods of detecting secu-
rity violations in networks. 
To create and to be able to: 
• use modern tools to monitor the state of the network; 
• use various methods to collect and process information about the state of the network; 
• use modern software for timely detection of known types of network attacks; 
• use modern methods of analytical data processing and discovering new knowledge in da-
tabases in the tasks of detecting information security violations; 
• use various methods to create and modify profiles of networks, nodes, users; 
• use profiles of networks, nodes, users to detect anomalies in the network; 
• apply well-known criteria to assess the effectiveness of systems for detecting information 
security violations in the network; 
• effectively use the obtained theoretical and practical knowledge for the analysis of infor-
mation security in networks 
To apply:  
Possession of modern methods and tools for detecting and preventing security breaches in the 
network. 
The process of studying the discipline is aimed at the formation of the following compe-
tencies: 
         Universal competencies (УК) 
         УК-6. Able to manage his time, build and implement the trajectory of self-develop-
ment based on the principles of education throughout life 
         Indicator 
 
6. Course content 
 Section 1. Collection and primary processing of information, network monitoring 
software. 
 Topic 1.1. Introduction. The concept of information security and methods of ensuring it. 
Network security and types of security breaches: network scanning, denial of service, unauthorized 
access, etc. 
 Topic 1.2. The Tcpdump package is the main tool for gathering information on the web. 
Tcpdump filters, signature analysis with Tcpdump package. An example of using the Tcpdump 
package to collect statistical information about network traffic. 
 Topic 1.3. Network packet headers, information from headers, types of attacks. TCP, UDP , 
IP, ICMP - packets, packet header fields, their admissible values and connection of header field 
values with possible network attacks. The most typical deviations of the cont ent of the headings 
from the normal values. 
 
Section 2. Methods for analyzing information and detecting violations 
 Topic 2.1. Violation detection model. General principles of building and organizing a sys-
tem for detecting security violations in a network. The concepts of a security subject, security 
object, system (network) activity and system (network) state audit. Activity mode l and metric of 
the system (network) state. Different types of activity patterns and methods for identifying security 
breaches in the network. 
 Topic 2.2. Intrusion detection methods. Signature methods and methods of analytical data 
processing. Machine learning methods, guided learning and self-learning methods. Supervised and 
Unsupervised methods of building a profile of the normal state of the system. Meth ods of classi-
fication, clustering, association and statistical methods for detecting anomalies. 
 Topic 2.3. Methodology for assessing the reliability and quality of security detection sys-
tems in the network. Standard types of metrics (True Negative, False Alarm, False Negative, Cor-
rectly detected attacks) used for assessing intrusion detection systems. 
 
 Section 3. Software tools for protecting information on the network. 
 Topic 3.1. NMAP is a network scanning tool. PORTSENTRY is a scan detection and pre-
vention program. 
 Topic 3.2. Network Security Zones: Intrnet, Demilitarized Zana, Trust Zone. Firewall is a 
means of dividing a network into zones. Packet filter IPTABLES. IPTABLES structure and filter-
ing rules. An example of a set of rules for IPTABLES. 
 Topic 3.2. SNORT is a software signature attack detection tool. Rules for generating filters 
of the SNORT system. Examples of SNORT filters to identify common types of network attacks. 
Examples of using a signature-based intrusion detection system 
7. Basic educational technologies 
When conducting lectures and laboratory classes, the following educational technologies are 
used: 
• multimedia lectures; 
• electronic forms of control; 
• self-testing of students. 
The educational process is based on the concept of competence -based learning, focused on 
the formation of a specific list of professional competencies, updating the theoretical knowledge 
obtained. The deployment of a competency-based learning model involves the widespread use of 
innovative ways of organizing the educational process, including the use of a project-based learn-
ing method, technologies of guided self -study, including a point-rating system, as well as the in-
troduction of an online support system for students' out-of-class work. 
8. Formative and Interim assessment methods 
Current control: attending lectures, performing laboratory work. 
Midterm control: performance of control tasks. 
Final certification: credit, set based on the results of work in the semester.

Programme description (annotation)  
 
Title of the programme: Theoretical Computer Science and Information 
Technologies (Фундаментальная информатика и информационные технологии) 
Department responsible for the programmе: I.I.Vorovich Institute of 
Mathematics, Mechanics and Computer Science, Southern Federal University  
Degree: Bachelor 
Duration: 4 years 
Number of ECTS: 240 
Number of places: 25  
Aim of the programme:  
In the academic sphere , the programme is aimed at training specialists in the field 
of theoretical and applied Informatics who are able to develop and promote computer 
science on the basis of existing and internationally recognized achievements and 
established practices. In the industrial fie ld, the program me trains specialists who, 
immediately after its completion, can be integrated into the existing industrial 
environment. In this direction, the program is focused on training specialists in 
creation and maintenance of complex information systems and services , use of 
advanced technologies, applied programming technologies and computer systems 
administration.  
In the learning process , students receive both basic knowledge related to the 
fundamental branches of computer science, such as theoretical algorithms and 
computability, as well as sections related to specific languages and programming 
systems. The mathematical and computer know ledge included in the program will 
help students independently conduct research work if they choose this path for their 
future activities.

name: Calculus (Непрерывная математика)
text:
ANNOTATION of the course  
Calculus (Непрерывная математика) 
Compiled by: A.V . Abramyan, Associate Professor of the Department of Informatics and 
Computational Experiment 
1. Program title, degree, study mode 
Direction of training: 02.03.02 "Theoretical Computer Science and Information Technolo-
gies" 
Graduate qualification (degree): Bachelor 
Full-time form of education 
2. Total load 
10 credits (360 hours), of which 68 hours of lectures, 84 hours of practical training and 208 
hours of independent work 
 
3. Course sequencing 
Academic discipline “Calculus (Непрерывная математика)" (1,2 courses, 2-3 semesters) 
belongs to the compulsory part of the block of disciplines and is compulsory. 
To study this academic discipline, there is enough knowledge, abilities and skills formed 
in the study of mathematical disciplines in a secondary school. 
The knowledge, skills and abilities obtained in the course of studying this discipline can 
be used to solve professional problems in research, scientific-production and design activities, in 
particular, in the development of algorithms and programs as part of the preparation of the final 
qualifying work. 
4. Course aims and objectives 
Acquaintance with various methods of research of variables, the basis of which is differ-
ential and integral calculus; acquaintance with the fundamental concepts and methods of re-
search of ordinary differential equations and equations of mathematical physics. 
Tasks:  
 mastering the technique of studying the convergence of sequences; 
 the study of methods for finding the limits of sequences and functions; 
 mastering the technique of differentiation and integration of functions in solving theoreti-
cal and applied problems;  
 acquiring the skills of studying the behavior of functions by methods of differential calcu-
lus; 
 mastering the technique of differentiating functions of several variables;  
 mastering the technique of solving basic types of ordinary differential equations; 
 mastering the technique of solving basic types of partial differential equations. 
5. Intended learning outcomes 
As a result of mastering the discipline, the student must have the following knowledge, 
skills and abilities: 
Knowledge:  
 basic mathematical concepts: set, function, limit, continuity, derivative, differentiability, dif-
ferential, antiderivative, integral sum, definite integral, numerical and functional series, con-
vergence of a series, open and closed sets, compactness; 
 formulations of the main statements of mathematical analysis; 
 basic concepts of the theory of differential equations: ordinary differential equation, partial 
differential equation, order of differential equation, general solution of differential equation, 
partial solution of differential equation, Cauchy problem, boundary value problem, funda-
mental systems of solutions, homogeneous and inhomogeneous differential equation, char-
acteristic equation; 
 formulations of the main statements of the theory of differential equations. 
Skills: 
 navigate elementary functions;  
 explore sequences, calculate limits;  
 investigate functions by methods of differential calculus; 
 apply differential calculus in geometry, physics; 
 explore numerical series for absolute and conditional convergence; 
 find expansions of functions in power series; 
 navigate the monographic literature on the theory of differential equations;  
 find a solution to the basic types of ordinary differential equations; 
 find a solution to the main types of partial differential equations; 
 construct a solution to the Cauchy problem and the boundary value problem 
Skills:  
 in the application of the technique of differentiation of functions; 
 in the application of the main methods of integration  
The process of studying the discipline is aimed at the formation of the following competencies: 
  OPK-1. Able to apply fundamental knowledge gained in the field of mathematical and (or) natu-
ral sciences, and use them in professional activities 
  Indicator 
  OPK-1.3. Solves standard math problems and applies their solutions in professional activities 
6. Course content 
Section 1. Limit of a numerical sequence 
Topic 1.1. Introduction 
Real numbers, gaps. The module of the number and its properties. Sign, floor and ceiling 
functions. Axiom of completeness. Bounded Sets, Top and Bottom Faces. Properties of bounded 
sets. The maximum (minimum) element, its uniqueness. Exact top (bottom) face (3 alternative 
definitions). Lemma on the existence and uniqueness of the exact upper bound. 
Topic 1.2. Sequences 
Determination of the sequence. Definition of a convergent sequence, a theorem on the 
uniqueness of the limit. Boundedness theorem for a converging sequence. A theorem on the mul-
tiplication of a converging sequence by a real number. The theorem on the sum, difference and 
product of converging sequences. A theorem on the properties of sequences related to inequali-
ties. Three consequences. Remark on the impossibility of replacing nonstrict inequalities by strict 
ones. Three-sequence theorem. An example of the application of the three sequences theorem: 
prove the convergence of a sequence 21

The quotient of converging sequences: a theorem on the convergence of a sequence {}1na; consequence of the quotient of converging sequences; an example of the application of the 
quotient theorem of converging sequences: lim nn a a  . 
Lemma on embedded segments.  
Infinitesimal sequences: definition; properties of infinitesimal sequences. Infinitely large 
sequences: definition; the relationship between infinitely small and infinitely large sequences. 
Monotone sequences. Basic definitions: (strictly) ascending sequence; (strictly) descend-
ing sequence; (strictly) monotone sequence. 
A criterion for the convergence of an increasing sequence. Four consequences. 
Topic 1.3. Subsequences. 
Definition of a subsequence. Subsequence element number property (kn  n). Sequence 
theorem for a converging sequence. Partial limit. Lemma Bolzano-Weierstrass. Upper and lower 
limit concepts. Determination of the fundamental sequence. Cauchy's criterion for the conver-
gence of a sequence. An example of the application of the Cauchy criterion: divergence of a 
harmonic sequence. 
Section 2. Functions of one variable (limit and continuity of a function). 
Topic 2.1. Function limit. 
Even and odd functions. Periodic functions. Limited features. Exact upper and exact 
bound of a function (two definitions). The maximum point and minimum point of the function. 
Neighborhood and- the neighborhood of the point. Gouged out the neighborhood and gouged 
out- the neighborhood of the point. Property of two (punctured) neighborhoods. 
Determination of the limit of a function. Limit uniqueness theorem. One-sided 
punctured- the neighborhood of the point. Limit on the left and limit on the right. A theorem on 
the connection between the existence of one-sided limits of a function at a point and the limit of 
a function at a point. Determination of the limit of a function atx→+∞ and at x→−∞... 
Limit properties: local boundedness of the function in the vicinity of the point at which 
the function has a limit; preservation of the sign of the function in the vicinity of the point at 
which the function has a limit that is not equal to zero; separation from zero of the values of the 
function in the vicinity of the point at which the function has a limit that is not equal to zero; the 
existence of a limit of the function 1 / f (x) in a neighborhood of the point at which the function f 
(x) has a nonzero limit. 
Arithmetic operations with limits: the limit of the sum of two functions; the limit of the 
product of two functions; the limit of the product of a function and a number; the limit of the dif-
ference between two functions; limit of the function 1 / f (x); the limit of the quotient of two 
functions. 
Two properties of limits related to inequalities. Analogue of the three-sequence theorem. 
Monotone functions. A theorem on the existence of one-sided limits of a monotone function on 
an interval. The first and second are remarkable limits. 
Infinitesimal functions. Properties of infinitesimal functions. Infinitely large functions. 
Relationship between infinitely large and infinitely small functions. 
Cauchy criterion for the existence of the limit of a function. Example: using the Cauchy 
criterion to prove that does not existlimx→0sin(1x)... 
Topic 2.1. Function limit. 
Definition of a continuous function. One-way continuity. Continuity in the gap. 
Breakpoint classification. Examples of functions having at a point: removable discontinu-
ity, irreparable discontinuity of the first kind, irreparable discontinuity of the second kind. 
Local properties of a function continuous at a point. Arithmetic operations with continu-
ous functions. Continuity theorem for a complex function. Weierstrass' theorem. Corollary on 
separating a function from zero. Theorem 1 on an intermediate value. Theorem 2 on an interme-
diate value. Three corollaries to intermediate value theorems. 
Definition of uniform continuity on the interval. Cantor's theorem. 
Inverse function existence theorem. 
Variable change theorem when calculating the limit. 
Equivalent functions. The theorem on the possibility of replacing (under the limit sign) a 
function by an equivalent function. Functions of the same order. Higher-order infinitesimal func-
tions. 
Section 3. Derivatives, Taylor's formula, study of a function using derivatives, gra-
phing functions 
Topic 3.1. Derivatives 
Definition of the derivative. Examples of calculating the derivatives of some functions. 
Example: functionf(x)=|x|has no derivative at zero. A theorem on the connection between the 
existence of a derivative and the continuity of a function. Continuous curve on a plane. Tangent. 
A theorem on the existence of a tangent at a point. One-sided derivatives. A theorem on the con-
nection between the existence at a point of a derivative and one-sided derivatives. 
Differentiability of the function. Differentiability of a function at a point. A criterion for 
the differentiability of a function at a point. Consequence. Differentiability of the function on the 
interval. Differentiation rules. Differential. Higher order derivatives. 
Fermat's theorem. Local minimum, strict local minimum. Local maximum, strict local 
maximum. Local extremum, strict local extremum. Rolle's theorem. Lagrange's theorem. Conse-
quence. Cauchy's theorem. 
Topic 3.2. L'Hôpital's rule 
L'Hôpital's rule. Uncertainty Disclosure Theorem(00) at x→a+0... Uncertainty Disclo-
sure Theorem(00) at x→+∞... Uncertainty Disclosure Theorem(∞∞)... 
Topic 3.3. Taylor's formula. 
Taylor's formula for a polynomial. Taylor's formula for an arbitrary function. Basic defi-
nitions. Lemma on the differentiation of the Taylor polynomial and the remainder. Remainder 
theorem in the Peano form. Lagrange Remainder Theorem. Corollary on the estimate of the re-
mainder in the Lagrange form. A theorem on the uniqueness of the expansion of a function in 
powers of a monomial. Consequence. 
 
Topic 3.4. Examining a function using derivatives. 
Conditions for the constancy and monotonicity of the function. Criterion (constant differ-
entiation). Consequence. The criterion for the increase (decrease) of the function. A criterion for 
strict increase (strict decrease) of a function + auxiliary lemma. Consequence. 
Extrema of functions. A necessary condition for an extremum. Stationary and critical 
points. A sufficient condition for an extremum in terms of the first derivative. A sufficient condi-
tion for an extremum in terms of the second derivative + auxiliary lemma. Sufficient condition 
for an extremum in terms of the nth derivative. 
Convex functions. Two definitions, geometric interpretation. A criterion for convexity 
and strict convexity of a function in terms of the first derivative. Two consequences. 
Inflection points. Definition. A necessary inflection condition. Sufficient inflection condi-
tion. 
Asymptotes. Determination of vertical, non-vertical, horizontal, oblique asymptotes. 
Criterion for the existence of a non-vertical asymptote. 
Section 4. Indefinite integral. Definite integral. 
Topic 4.1. Indefinite integral 
Definition of antiderivative. A sufficient condition for the existence of an antiderivative 
on an interval. Theorem on the set of all antiderivatives. The concept of an indefinite integral. 
Three properties of indefinite integrals. Change of variables in the indefinite integral. Integration 
by parts. Integration of rational functions. 
Topic 4.2. Definite integral 
Definition of the Riemann integral. An example of calculating a definite integral based on 
its definition. A necessary condition for the integrability of a function. An example of the fact 
that the boundedness condition is not sufficient for the integrability of a function (Dirichlet func-
tion). Determination of the upper and lower Darboux sums. Four properties of Darboux sums. A 
criterion for the integrability of a function. Determination of fluctuation of a function. Three 
properties of fluctuations of a function An alternative formulation of the criterion for integrabil-
ity of a function. Four properties of integrable functions. 
Sufficient conditions for the integrability of functions: the theorem on the integrability of 
a monotone function; a theorem on the integrability of a function that is continuous on a seg-
ment; a corollary on the integrability of a function that is continuous on an interval and has one-
sided limits at its ends. 
Properties of the definite integral as a function of the interval of integration. A theorem on 
the representation of an integral over [a, c] as a sum of integrals over [a, b] and [b, c] in the case 
a <b <c. Definition ∫baf(x)dx, a<b and  ∫aaf(x)dx... Corollary on the representation of the inte-
gral over [a, c] as a sum of integrals over [a, b] and [b, c] in the casea, b, cR. 
A theorem on the integrability of a piecewise continuous function. An estimate theorem 
for the integral of a nonnegative function. Consequence. Mean value theorem for a definite inte-
gral. Consequence. 
Function differentiation theorem F(x)= ∫cxf(t)dt... Corollary on the existence of a con-
tinuous antiderivative. Corollary: Newton-Leibniz formula. 
Change of variable theorem in a definite integral. Integration by parts theorem. 
Section 5. Numerical series 
Topic 5.1. Basic definitions 
Number series, partial sum, series term, converging / diverging series, remainder of the 
series. Examples of investigating the convergence of numerical series. Four properties of number 
series. 
Topic 5.2. Rows with non-negative terms 
A criterion for the convergence of series with non-negative terms. Comparison of rows. 
Examples of using the comparison feature to study the convergence of numerical series. 
D'Alembert's sign. Cauchy sign. Comparison of D'Alembert and Cauchy signs. Integral feature. 
An example of using an integral feature to study the convergence of a series. 
Topic 5.3. Rows with arbitrary members. 
Definition of an absolutely convergent series, a conditionally convergent series. Two 
properties of converging series. 
Alternating rows. Definition of alternating series. Leibniz's sign. An example of the ap-
plication of the Leibniz criterion. 
Dirichlet test. Abel's sign. 
Section 6. Improper integral. 
Definition and properties of improper integrals. 
Improper integral of non-negative functions. Convergence criteria for an improper inte-
gral in the general case. 
Properties of the improper integral as a function of the interval of integration. Average 
theorem. Newton-Leibniz formula. 
Section 7. Functions of several variables 
Limit and Continuity. Partial derivatives. Differentiability of the function. Differential. 
Derivative and differential of a complex function. Partial derivatives and differentials of higher 
orders. Implicit functions and their differentiation. Extremes. Conditional extremum. Directional 
derivative. Gradient. 
Section 8. Ordinary differential equations 
Definition. Properties of solutions to a linear differential equation. Cauchy problem. 
Homogeneous differential equations (ODE). A criterion for linear independence of a sys-
tem of solutions to a homogeneous equation. Fundamental decision system. The theorem on the 
existence of a fundamental system of solutions (FSS). A theorem on representing the solution of 
an ODE in the form of a linear combination of functions from the FSR. Homogeneous equation 
with constant coefficients. Characteristic polynomial. The FSR theorem in the case when the 
characteristic polynomial has no multiple roots. The FSR theorem in the case when the charac-
teristic polynomial has multiple roots. 
Method of variation of arbitrary constants. 
Particular solution in the case of the right side of a special type. 
7. Basic educational technologies 
When conducting lectures and practical classes, the following educational technologies are 
used: 
 multimedia lectures; 
 testing of students. 
The educational process is based on the concept of competence-based learning, focused on 
the formation of a specific list of professional competencies, updating the theoretical knowledge 
obtained. The deployment of a competency-based learning model involves the widespread use of 
innovative ways of organizing the educational process, including the use of a project-based 
learning method, technologies of guided self-study, including a point-rating system, as well as 
the introduction of an online support system for students' out-of-class work. 
8. Formative and Interim assessment methods 
Current control: attendance of lectures, performance of verification works. 
Midterm control: control works. 
Final certification: exam.

text:
ANNOTATION of the course  
2024 ru-ANN-Linear Algebra and Geometry (Линейная алгебра и геометрия) 
 
 
Compiled by: Professor of the Department of Algebra and Discrete Mathematics Ya.M. Erusalim-
sky 
 
1. Program title, degree, study mode 
Direction of training: 02.03.02 "Theoretical Computer Science and Information Technolo-
gies" 
Qualification (degree) of the graduate: bachelor 
Form of study: full-time 
 
2. Total load 
10 credits (360 hours), of which 86 hours of lectures, 68 hours of practical training, 90 hours 
of independent work and 108 hours of exam preparation 
 
3. Course sequencing 
Academic discipline “Linear Algebra and Geometry (Линейная алгебра и геометрия)” re-
fers to the mandatory part of the discipline block. To study this academic discipline, knowledge of 
mathematics, computer science and the basics of ICT, acquired in high school, is required. 
The list of subsequent academic disciplines for which knowledge, skills and abilities are 
required, formed by this academic discipline: 
«Mathematical Logic ( Математическая логика)», « Automata Theory and Formal Lan-
guages ( Теория автоматов и формальных языков)», « Algorithms and Data Structures 
(Алгоритмы и структуры данных)», « Expert Systems and Non -classical Logic ( Экспертные 
системы и неклассические логики)», «Probability Theory and Mathematical Statistics (Теория 
вероятностей и математическая статистика)» and others. 
4. Course aims and objectives 
Developing students' competencies in using the apparatus of algebra and geometry in solving 
their professional problems. 
Tasks:  
- Assistance in the formation of a comprehensively developed personality as a subject of 
successful professional, educational and research activities.  
- Formation of students' ideas about the place of algebra and geometry in the system of 
mathematical disciplines and their applications, about their connections with discrete mathematics, 
mathematical analysis, probability theory and mathematical statistics, computer cycle disciplines, 
etc. 
- Formation of professional competencies of a bachelor, associated with the use of mathe-
matical models of processes and objects, the development of effective mathematical methods for 
solving algebraic and geometric problems. 
 
5. Intended learning outcomes 
As a result of mastering the discipline, the student must: 
Know: basic concepts and objects of linear algebra and geometry: vectors, matrices, deter-
minants, systems of linear equations, complex numbers, equations of lines, planes, curves of the 
second order, linear spaces and subspaces, linear operators and their matrices, Euclidean spaces, 
bilinear and quadratic forms ...  
Be able to: compose equations of basic geometric objects (straight lines, planes, curves of 
the 2nd order), solve SLU and OSLU, operate with matrices, calculate determinants, work with 
complex numbers and polynomials, calculate the rank of a matrix and use it to fin d the basis and 
dimension of the lin. shell. Operate with matrices of linear operators, find eigenvectors and eigen-
values, factorize polynomials in terms of roots, carry out the orthogonalization process, reduce 
bilinear forms to diagonal form, reduce quadratic forms to canonical and normal forms. 
Own: tools and methods of algebra and geometry and the ability to apply them in solving 
practical problems. 
The process of studying the discipline is aimed at the formation of the following competen-
cies: 
  General professional competences (ОПК) 
  ОПК-1. Able to apply fundamental knowledge gained in the field of mathematical and (or) natural 
sciences, and use them in professional activities 
  Indicator 
  ОПК-1.2. Applies the basic terminology of mathematical sciences and mathematical objects when 
solving problems of professional activity 
 
6. Course content 
Module 1. Analytical geometry on a plane 
Analytical geometry on a straight line. Numerical line, directional segment, its size and 
length, properties of the magnitude of the directed segment. Division of a segment in a given ratio. 
Midpoint of the segment. Coordinate systems in the plane and in space. Polar and Cartesian coor-
dinates, the relationship between them. Cartesian coordinate transformations: shift, rotation, gen-
eral transformation. 
The concept of equations for lines and surfaces, types of equations: explicit, general, para-
metric. Straight line on a plane. Equations of a straight line, distance from a point to a straight line, 
the theorem on the division of a plane by the general equation of a straight line. 
Curves of the second order are their canonical. Equations. Tangents to curves of the second 
order. Touch conditions 
Module 2. SLS, matrix algebra, determinants 
Matrices, their types, operations on matrices and their properties. Matrix multiplication and 
its properties. The powers of a square matrix. Reversibility and one -way reversibility. Zero divi-
sors, a necessary condition for invertibility, the existence of r eversible and irreversible matrices. 
Group of invertible matrices. Polynomials in a matrix, The simplest matrix equations. 
SLU and SLU. SLN classification. Gaussian transformations of the SLN. Gauss method. 
Substitutions and permutations and their characteristics. Permutation composition. Permu-
tation recording. Permutation group. Group homomorphism. 
Determinants. Three definitions of the determinant and their equivalence. Determinant 
properties. Minors and algebraic complements. Laplace's theorem. The theorem on the determinant 
of the product of matrices. The criterion for the equality to zero of the determinant. Attached ma-
trix. Matrix invertibility criterion. Cramer's theorem and a corollary from it. Determinant of Van-
dermonde. 
Module 3. Complex numbers and polynomials 
Algebraic form of a complex number and operations on k.h. Geometric interpretation of 
c.ch. and tr. form k.h. Operations on k.ch. in trigon. form. Moivre's formula. Division in a set of 
c.ch. Module and argument properties. Roots from complex numbers. Root s from one. Primitive 
roots. A group of roots from one. 
Polynomials. Uniqueness theorem. Operations on polynomials. Division in the set of pol-
ynomials. Division with remainder. GCD. Euclid's Algorithm. Roots of polynomials. Bezout's the-
orem and its consequences. Root expansion. Multiplicity of the root. Vieta's theorem. Polynomials 
with real coefficients and their roots, decomposition into irreducible factors. Polynomials with 
integer and rational coefficients. Integer and rational roots of polynomials with rational and integer 
coefficients. Derivative of a polynomial. The roots of the polynomial and derivative. Construction 
of a polynomial with single roots. 
Module 4. Analytical geometry in space 
Vectors and operations on them. Decomposition of a vector into non-coplanar vectors. Vec-
tor coordinates and dot product. Vector product of vectors. Vector product coordinates. Mixed 
product of vectors. The coordinate form for the mixed work. Conditions for collinearity, orthogo-
nality and coplanarity of vectors. 
Plane and straight line in space. Equation of a plane passing through three points. Equation 
of a plane passing through a point and having a given normal vector. General equation of the plane. 
Geom. the meaning of its coefficients. Special equations of the plane. Distance from point to plane. 
A bundle of planes. Equations of a straight line passing through a point in a given direction. Para-
metric equations of a straight line. Straight line as intersection of planes. Distance from point to 
line problem 
Module 5. Linear spaces 
Linear spaces. Definition of l.p. and examples. Systems of vectors in lp Linear combina-
tion. Linearly dependent and linearly independent systems of vectors and their properties. Com-
plete systems of vectors. Basis and dimension. Vector coordinates. Transition from basis to basis. 
Transition matrix. Properties of transition matrices. Finding the transition matrix. Linear sub-
spaces. Linear hull as a subspace. Linear shell properties. Sum and intersection of linear subspaces. 
Dimension theorem. The direct sum and the criterion are straightforward. The rank of the matrix. 
Rank definitions. Rank properties. Matching ranks. Application of rank to SLU and OSLU. FSR. 
Module 6. Linear operators. Quadratic forms 
Linear operators in linear spaces. Definition and examples of lin. operators. The core and 
the image, and their properties. Matrix of a linear operator in finite-dimensional spaces. Transition 
from bases to bases. Kernel and image dimensions. Operator rank . Theorem on dim ker A + dim 
Im A. The space of linear operators. Algebra L (X, X). Lin degrees. operator. Subalgebras of the 
algebra L (X, X). Invertibility in the algebra L (X, X). Eigenvectors and eigenvalues of lin. opera-
tor. Characteristic polynomial. Lin theorem. independence of eigenvectors corresponding to dif-
ferent eigenvalues. Influence on the lin matrix. operator presence in the basis of its eigenvectors. 
Simple spectrum operator 
Euclidean spaces. Definition and examples. Vector length. Angle between vectors. Ner-vo 
K.-B. Ner-in Minkowski. Pythagorean theorem. Orthogonal systems and their sv-va. Orthonormal 
systems. Advantages of Orthogonal and Orthonormal Systems. Parseval's equality. Vector coordi-
nates in orthonormal basis. Orthogonalization process. Orthogonal direct sum. Orthogonal direct 
sum decomposition. Projection and orthogonal component. Distance from vector to subspace. Or-
thogonal complement and its sv-va. Problem of projection and orthogonal component. Orthogonal 
matrices and their properties. Gram matrix and determinant. The adjoint operator and its matrix. 
Self-adjoint operators and their properties. Invariant subspaces and invariance of ort. additions to 
them for s.s. operator. Reality of the spectrum of s.s. operator. Diagonalizability of the matrix s.s. 
operator. 
Bilinear and quadratic forms. Definition of b.l.f. and matrix b.l.f. Relationship between ma-
trices b.l.f. in different bases. Symmetrical b.l.f. Canonical theorem. form and canonical. basis for 
a symmetric b.l.f. Quadratic forms and their matrices. Symmetr ic notation of the square form. 
Numerical characteristics of sq. forms. Theorems on reducibility to canonical and normal forms. 
Criteria for positive and negative certainty. Sylvester's criterion (without proof). 
 
7. Basic educational technologies 
When conducting classes, such educational technologies are used as classical lectures, prob-
lem lectures; work in small groups - performing tasks in the classroom with a preliminary collec-
tive discussion of the topic; individual tasks (home and classroom). 
Classroom and extracurricular work is organized on the basis of an individual and differen-
tiated approach to students. The educational process is based on the concept of competence-based 
learning, focused on the formation of a specific list of professional competencies, updating the 
theoretical knowledge obtained. The deployment of a competency-based learning model involves 
the widespread use of innovative ways of organizing the educational process, incl. application of 
the project-based teaching method, technologies of guided self-teaching, including the point-rating 
system. 
 
8. Formative and Interim assessment methods 
Current control: homework. 
Mid-term control: test papers. 
Final examination: exam.

name: Algorithms and Data Structures
text:
ANNOTATION of the course 
Algorithms and Data Structures  
(Алгоритмы и структуры данных) 
Compiled by: Senior Lecturer of the Department of Applied Mathemati cs and Programming 
M.V. Puchkin 
1. Program title, degree, study mode 
Direction of training: 02.03.02 Theoretical Computer Science and Information Technologies 
(Фундаментальная информатика и информационные технологии) 
Graduate qualification (degree): Bachelor 
Full-time form of education 
2. Total load 
5 credits (180 hours), of which 48 hours of lectures, 16 hours of laboratory studies and 4 4 
hours of independent work, 72 hours of exam preparation 
3. Course sequencing 
Academic discipline “ Algorithms and Data Structures (Алгоритмы и структуры 
данных)” (2 course, 4 semester) refers to a part of a block of disciplines (modules) formed by 
participants in educational relations, and is a compulsory discipline. 
To study this academic discipline, knowledge, skills and abilities are required that are 
formed by the previous disciplines: 
“Basics of Programming (Основы программирования)"(1 course, 1-2 semesters); 
“Discrete Mathematics (Дискретная математика)" (1 course, 1-2 semesters). 
Discipline “ Algorithms and Data Structures "is designed to provide the formation of 
knowledge, skills and abilities that are necessary or in demand in the study of many subsequent 
(studied from 4 to 8 semesters) disciplines, including: 
“ Computer Graphics (Компьютерная графика)"; 
“Introduction to Machine Learning and Neural Networks ( Введение в машинное обуче-
ние и нейронные сети)". 
Depending on the directions and structure of master's programs, this course may be the 
basis for further in -depth training in such areas as "Image Analysis and Processing", "Neural 
Networks", "Artificial Intelligence", etc. The knowledge and skills gained in the course of study-
ing this discipline can be used to solve professional problems in research, scientific production 
and design activities, in particular, when developing programs as part of graduation qualification 
works. 
4. Course aims and objectives 
Acquaintance with the principles of construction and analysis of algorithms, introduction of 
basic concepts, consideration of basic and specialized data structures with an emphasis on the 
practical side of solving applied problems. Development of students' competencies related to the 
development of highly loaded information systems for data processing using adequate and effec-
tive algorithms - systems for mathematical modeling, numerical calculations, simulation sys-
tems, systems for analysis and processing of texts, databases, and the like. At the same time, the 
goal of in-depth study of the mathematical foundations of the theory of algorithms is not set, the 
main goal is to present the general concepts of this discipline to students, as well as, if possible, 
the most versatile coverage of a set of practical problems, indicating the most suitable data struc-
tures and algorithms for implementation. 
Tasks:  
– Studying the basic principles of evaluating algorithms - efficiency, speed, correctness, etc 
.; 
– Mastering the methods of empirical (practical) assessment of the effectiveness of data 
structures and algorithms; 
– Study of basic data structures, methods of their implementation using general -purpose 
programming languages; 
– Consideration of a wide range of typical tasks (for example, representing graphs or pro-
cessing strings), indicating the corresponding families of algorithms, developing an un-
derstanding that the effectiveness of algorithms is correct to consider and compare only 
within the framework of a specific task; 
– Building a "data structure map", with consideration of typical basic and derived struc-
tures, indicating their characteristics and areas of application; 
– Developing the ability to design and implement software systems and complexes, taking 
into account the features and selection of appropriate tools, simple and composite data 
structures, as well as algorithms; 
– Mastering the skills of using specialized libraries, weaning from the habit of “reinventing 
the wheel” and implementing complex software systems “from scratch”; 
– Consideration of the elements of the standard library of templates of the C ++ program-
ming language, as well as specialized libraries - CryptoPP, Boost and others. 
5. Intended learning outcomes 
As a result of mastering the discipline, the student must have the following knowledge, 
skills and abilities: 
To understand and analyze:  
• basic algorithmic solutions and general purpose algorithms; 
• approaches to evaluating the effectiveness of algorithms; 
To create and to be able to: 
• develop complex software systems, including several subsystems, using various libraries 
/ programming languages in various problems of applied programming; 
To apply:  
• specification of requirements for software solutions; 
• evaluating the effectiveness and applicability of various algorithms; 
• using collaborative development tools like GitHub. 
 
The process of studying the discipline is aimed at the formation of the following competen-
cies: 
 General professional competences (ОПК) 
 ОПК-3. Capable of developing algorithmic and software solutions in the fieldsystem  and appli-
cation programming, mathematical, information and simulation models, creation of information 
resources of global networks, educational content, application databases, tests and testing tools 
for systems and tools for compliance with standards and initial requirements 
 Indicator 
 ОПК-3.1. Applies methods of the theory of algorithms, methods of system and ap-
pliedprogramming, fundamentals and concepts in the field of mathematical, information and 
simulation models 
6. Course content 
Section 1. Introduction to Algorithm Analysis 
Topic 1.1. Fundamentals of Algorithm Analysis. Asymptotic analysis, O-notation 
Algorithm evaluation criteria, spatial and temporal complexity, input dependence. Diffi-
culty at best, worst and average. Asymptotic estimates, comparison of functions, O -notation. Ex-
amples of time spent on algorithms with different complexity, complexity analysis using the ex-
ample of a sorting algorithm. 
Topic 1.2. Recurrence relations and analysis of recurrent algorithms. The main the-
orem on recurrence relations 
Recurrence relations as a means of analyzing recurrent algorithms using simple merge 
sort as an example. Substitution methods, variable substitutions, recursion trees. The main theo-
rem on recurrence relations and examples of its application. 
Topic 1.3. Practical methods of comparative analysis of algorithms 
Features of measuring the time spent on executing algorithms in various programming 
languages. Comparative analysis of programming languages, techniques for debugging and op-
timization, "clean" application launch, measuring the running time of program fragments in C 
++. 
Section 2. Basic data structures 
Topic 2.1. Dynamic data structures - lists, trees. Implementation of abstract data 
types - queues and stack 
Linear lists - singly and doubly linked, use for the implementation of the stack and queue, 
estimate memory costs. Multi-linked lists, memory saving strategies, deque. Graphs, trees - trees 
with order on children, ways of representing "left child" - "right sibling". Trees with parent ref-
erences only. 
Topic 2.2. Tree dynamic structures - binary trees, branch trees, search trees 
Binary trees, representations, search trees, perfectly balanced trees. Basic operations and 
their evaluation, examples of use. 
Topic 2.3. Self-balancing trees. AVL, RBT and B-trees. Set Representation 
Trees with maintenance of balance in height and number of elements. Maintaining order 
and balance, rotation operations. Algorithm for adding a vertex to a red -black tree, general ideas 
of algorithms for removing a vertex from RBT, as well as operations with AVL trees. Compari-
son of the asymptoti cs of depth, counting the number of rotations. B -trees, implementation and 
usage features, B-tree growth scheme. Operations of adding and removing vertices for B-trees. 
Topic 2.4 Systems of disjoint sets 
Operations with disjoint sets, disadvantages of self -balancing trees for the implementa-
tion of such sets. An implementation with an efficient operation of combining two sets. Path 
compression heuristic, weight heuristic. 
Topic 2.5 Heaps (pyramids) - binary, fibonacci, binomial 
Binary heaps, basic operations, array based heap representation. Evaluating operations, 
sorting with a binary heap, a heap -based priority queue. General ideas of binomial heap, imple-
mentation of merge operation of two heaps, and also element extraction. Evaluation of opera-
tions. Binomial heaps, heuristics, lazy ordering idea. Advanced priority queue. 
Topic 2.6. Hash functions and hash tables. Comparison with trees 
Definition of a hash function, requirements for hash functions, the difference from cryp-
tographic ones. Collisions. Methods for representing sets using direct addressing, open address-
ing, and chaining. Kinds of hash functions - based on multiplication, based on division. Clusters 
of the first and second kind, universal hashing. Comparison of the efficiency of hash tables and 
tree-based sets, hash functions for strings. 
Section 3. Approaches to the construction and optimization of enumeration algo-
rithms 
Topic 3.1. Greedy algorithms in enumeration problems, search strategies. Back-
tracking (brute force with backtracking). Examples of tasks 
Enumeration algorithms, greedy algorithms and signs of their applicability. Scheduling 
problem, continuous knapsack problem. Backtracking on the example of the knight travel prob-
lem. Heuristics in enumeration problems, efficiency and implementation issues. 
Topic 3.2 Dynamic programming. Matrix multiplication problems, the largest 
common subsequence. Branch and bound method 
General concepts of dynamic programming, top -down and bottom -up strategies, mem-
oization. Optimality principle for subproblems, comparison with the class of greedy algorithms. 
Matrix multiplication problems, the largest common subsequence, the placement of parentheses. 
Recursion based and array based implementation, solution recovery. 
Topic 3.3. Depreciation analysis 
Booked transaction costs, group analysis, amortized cost, potential method. Applicability 
- problems about a binary counter, about adding elements to an array, about a polystek. 
Section 4. Additional sections - substring search, computational geometry, graph al-
gorithms 
Topic 4.1. Graph representation. Graph search strategies, typical tasks 
Dense and sparse graphs, presentation methods using lists of adjacent vertices and adja-
cency matrices. Depth -first search and breadth -first search strategies, recursive and iterative im-
plementations. Topological sorting algorithm. The shortest path problem for a pair of vertices. 
Spanning trees, Kruskal and Prim's algorithms. Tools for working with graphs in C ++ (Boost 
Graph Library, a brief overview). 
Topic 4.2. Substring search algorithms 
The task of finding substrings, estimation relative to the size of the pattern and the input 
string. An agreement on the probabilities of a pattern, a naive search algorithm, an average, 
worst-case and best -case estimate. Rabin -Karp algorithm, dependence of efficiency on the size 
of a machine word. Search for substrings using state machines. Suffix and prefix functions, 
Knuth-Morris-Pratt algorithm. Bower -Moore Algorithm, Stop Symbol and Safe Suffix Heuris-
tics. Comparison of algorithms. 
Topic 4.3. Computational geometry. Representation of points and segments, convex 
hull problems, visualization 
Representation of points on the plane and in space, convex hulls - definition, algorithms 
of Jarvis and Graham. Performance evaluation, presentation and visualization tools using visual 
components of the Qt platform (overview). 
 
Questions for self-study 
As such, tasks appear for the implementation of applications with a graphical interface in 
the Qt 5.6.0 development environment or higher, with the obligatory use of specialized libraries 
for working with data structures. For example, when studying the topic "Representation of 
graphs", students are offered as an additional task to implement an application with a graphical 
interface using the BGL library. 
Also, in the process of studying this discipline, students are encouraged to solve problems of 
computational mathemati cs, for example, from the collection "Project Euler": 
https://projecteuler.net... These problems require some mathematical training, but they are de-
signed to be solved using computer technology, and the problems are selected in such a way that 
an ineffective algorithm or sloppy implementation provides unacceptable running time. 
7. Basic educational technologies 
When conducting lectures and laboratory classes, the following educational technologies 
are used: 
- multimedia lectures; 
- electronic forms of control; 
- self-testing of students; 
- teamwork of students in the implementation of game tasks. 
 
The educational process is based on the concept of competence -based learning, focused 
on the formation of a specific list of professional competencies, updating the theoretical 
knowledge obtained. The deployment of a competence -based learning model involves the wide-
spread use of innovative ways of organizing the educational process, incl. application of the pro-
ject-based teaching method, technologies of guided self -study, including the point-rating system, 
as well as the introduction of an online support system for students' out-of-class work. 
 
8. Formative and Interim assessment methods  
Current control: attending lectures, performing laboratory work. 
Mid-term control: testing, completing additional tasks. 
Final attestation: exam, grade is set based on the results of a written exam, oral questioning 
as part of the exam is not provided.
